name: Belly Down Armbar from New York
description: Master the belly down armbar finish from New York rubber guard. Learn overhook arm isolation, prone rotation mechanics, and high-leverage finishing details.
target_area: Elbow joint hyperextension and ulnar collateral ligament
summary: The Belly Down Armbar from New York is a 10th Planet Rubber Guard finish where the bottom player converts a deep overhook into arm isolation, rotates belly-down, and hyperextends the trapped elbow between their thighs for a high-leverage tap.
overview:
The belly down armbar finish from New York leverages the deep overhook control inherent to 10th Planet's Rubber Guard system to isolate and hyperextend the opponent's elbow from a mechanically dominant prone position. Unlike standard armbar finishes where the attacker remains supine with hips elevated, the belly down variation rotates the attacker face-down on the mat, creating a wedge effect against the trapped elbow that is extraordinarily difficult to defend once fully locked. The overhook established in New York provides the initial arm isolation that makes this transition seamlessly available without the typical armbar setup sequence of fighting for wrist control.

The strategic value of this finish from New York specifically lies in the element of deception and the smooth transition from guard retention to submission. Most opponents defending New York anticipate choke setups toward Invisible Collar or leg-based transitions to Chill Dog and Zombie. The armbar path catches defenders oriented toward the wrong threat axis entirely. The overhook already accomplishes the hardest part of any armbar attack: trapping and isolating a single arm away from the defender's centerline, meaning the attacker can skip directly to leg positioning and rotation.

Biomechanically, the belly down finish multiplies the attacker's leverage by converting hip bridge force into rotational torque against the hyperextended elbow. The prone position eliminates the most common armbar escape where the defender stacks the attacker and extracts the arm overhead. Once the rotation is complete and the attacker is face-down with the arm pinned between their thighs, the defender has no viable stacking angle and the mechanical advantage ratio exceeds 5:1 against the elbow joint. The finishing pressure requires minimal energy since gravity assists rather than opposes the extension force.

injury_risks.injury: Elbow hyperextension with ligament damage to the ulnar collateral ligament
Elbow joint capsule sprain or partial tear from forced extension
Biceps tendon strain or partial tear from resisting extension under load
Distal humerus stress fracture from sustained pressure against locked elbow

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive. The belly down position creates significant mechanical advantage that can damage the elbow extremely quickly. Apply extension gradually and allow adequate time for the tap. Never jerk or spike the arm. The prone position amplifies force beyond what most practitioners expect.
tap_signals: Verbal tap saying 'tap' or any distress vocalization
Physical hand tap on partner, mat, or own body
Physical foot tap on mat with either leg
Any screaming, grunting, or unusual vocalization indicating distress
release_protocol: Release immediately upon any tap signal without waiting for confirmation or repetition
If in doubt whether a tap occurred, release immediately - the position can be re-established safely
Release extension pressure first by lowering the wrist, then release knee squeeze, then disengage completely
Monitor training partner's arm mobility after release and check for signs of injury before continuing
training_restrictions: Beginners should practice mechanics at 50% pressure maximum until transition control is consistent
Always apply extension slowly in training - never jerk or spike the arm during the belly down finish
Do not apply this technique on training partners with known elbow injuries or recent arm submissions
Practice the transition rotation separately from the finishing pressure until both components are reliable

variations_and_setups.description: From established New York, convert the deep overhook directly into arm isolation by shooting the outside leg over the opponent's head while maintaining the overhook grip. The most common and highest-percentage entry because the overhook already has the arm trapped.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent is passive in New York and not actively fighting the overhook

variations_and_setups.description: Threaten the triangle by shooting your leg over the opponent's shoulder, then when they defend the triangle by posturing, redirect to armbar by clamping the isolated arm and rotating belly down. Uses the triangle threat to create the opening for the armbar.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent is actively defending against choke threats and pulling their head back

variations_and_setups.description: Use a hip bump from New York to off-balance the opponent forward, then as they post with their free hand to resist, clamp the overhook arm with your legs and rotate belly down in one fluid motion. The hip bump creates urgency that prevents the opponent from extracting the trapped arm.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent has strong posture and is resisting the standard armbar entry

attacker.name: from New York Attacker
attacker.description: Execute the belly down armbar from New York rubber guard. Step-by-step overhook isolation, prone rotation, and elbow hyperextension finishing mechanics.
attacker.overview: Attacking the belly down armbar from New York requires converting your existing overhook control into full arm isolation, then executing a precise rotation to the prone finishing position. The key advantage of this attack path is that New York's deep overhook already eliminates the most difficult phase of armbar attacks: isolating a single arm from the defender's centerline. Your primary challenge is maintaining arm control during the transition from guard to belly down while preventing the opponent from retracting the trapped arm or recovering posture. The rotation itself must be committed and smooth, because hesitation during the belly down turn creates extraction windows that experienced defenders will exploit immediately.
key_principles: The overhook must be deep around the tricep before initiating the armbar sequence - shallow overhooks allow extraction during transition
Leg positioning over the opponent's head must happen before releasing the shin grip to prevent posture recovery
Commit fully to the belly down rotation once initiated - half-rotations create escape opportunities
Squeeze knees together throughout the entire sequence to maintain arm isolation during all transition phases
Control the wrist with both hands before rotating - losing wrist control during the turn allows the opponent to bend their elbow and escape
Use hip movement rather than upper body torque to drive the belly down rotation for maximum control retention
Apply finishing pressure through hip elevation against the mat, not by pulling the arm - let gravity assist the hyperextension
setup_requirements: Deep overhook secured around the opponent's tricep with your shoulder tight against their armpit in established New York control
Opponent's posture fully broken with their head at chest level, preventing explosive posture recovery during transition
Shin across the opponent's back maintained until ready to shoot the leg over for arm isolation
Core engaged and hips angled toward the overhook side to facilitate the leg swing and subsequent rotation
Free hand ready to transition from shin grip to wrist control during the arm isolation phase

execution_steps.description: Verify your overhook is deep around the opponent's tricep with your shoulder tight against their armpit. Ensure your shin is high across their back with a firm ankle grip. Break their posture completely so their head is level with your chest. Do not initiate the armbar sequence until all three control points are solid and the opponent is unable to posture up.
execution_steps.timing: 2-4 seconds to verify all control points

execution_steps.action: Shoot outside leg over opponent's head
execution_steps.description: Release your shin grip and swing your outside leg up and over the opponent's head, placing your calf across the back of their neck. Maintain the deep overhook throughout this movement to prevent the opponent from posturing during the leg transition. Your hip must elevate to create clearance for the leg, and the movement should be smooth rather than explosive to avoid losing the overhook connection.

Squeeze both legs together tightly around the isolated arm, positioning the opponent's elbow directly against your hip bone as the primary fulcrum point. Your knees must pinch inward to prevent any arm rotation or extraction. The trapped arm should be oriented thumb-up between your thighs with the elbow crease facing your hips, ensuring the hyperextension force will apply correctly when you finish.

Release the overhook grip and immediately secure the opponent's wrist with both hands, pulling the arm tight against your chest. Use a two-on-one grip with your thumbs pointing toward their fingers and your palms wrapping the wrist. This bilateral wrist control prevents them from bending their elbow to relieve pressure and is essential before initiating the belly down rotation where grip security becomes critical.
execution_steps.timing: 1 second transition from overhook to wrist grip

execution_steps.description: Shrimp your hips away from the opponent while maintaining the thigh clamp and wrist control, creating an angle perpendicular to their body. This angular displacement increases your leverage on the elbow and removes the opponent's ability to stack you by driving forward. Keep constant tension pulling the wrist toward your chest throughout the hip escape to prevent any elbow bend during your repositioning movement.

Commit to the belly down rotation by turning face-down toward the mat while keeping the arm pinned tightly between your thighs. Drive the rotation with your hips rather than your shoulders to maintain leg squeeze pressure throughout the turn. The rotation must be smooth and continuous, not jerky, to prevent the opponent from finding an extraction window during the transition. Your chest should end facing the mat with the opponent's arm still thumb-up between your legs.

With your face toward the mat and the opponent's arm trapped thumb-up between your thighs, elevate your hips upward in a controlled bridge motion while pulling their wrist toward your chest. This creates hyperextension pressure against the elbow joint using your hip line as the fulcrum. Apply pressure gradually and progressively, allowing adequate time for the tap signal. The prone position generates extreme mechanical advantage, so minimal hip elevation produces significant force on the joint.
execution_steps.timing: 2-3 seconds of gradual progressive pressure until tap

common_counters.counter: Arm extraction before leg clamp - opponent pulls elbow back toward their hip as you release the shin grip
common_counters.your_response: Maintain overhook pressure until the leg is fully over their head before releasing. If they begin extraction, immediately re-secure the overhook and reset to New York rather than chasing a loose arm. Alternatively, transition to triangle setup since their arm withdrawal creates the inside position needed for the triangle lock.

common_counters.counter: Stack and pressure pass - opponent drives forward explosively during the transition to flatten the attacker and pass guard
common_counters.your_response: If they stack before you complete the belly down rotation, use the stacking momentum to accelerate your rotation in the opposite direction, pulling them into the belly down position. Keep your legs clamped and wrist control tight through the stack. If the stack is too strong, release and recover to closed guard to prevent the pass.

common_counters.counter: Hitchhiker escape - opponent rotates their thumb toward the mat and spins their body toward the trapped arm during or after the belly down rotation
common_counters.your_response: Follow their rotation by adjusting your hip angle to maintain perpendicular alignment to their arm. Squeeze your knees tighter and re-center the elbow against your hip fulcrum. The belly down position actually makes the hitchhiker less effective than against a standard armbar because you can pin their rotating shoulder with your body weight.

common_counters.counter: Hand clasping defense - opponent grabs their own wrist or bicep to prevent arm extension
common_counters.your_response: The belly down position makes hand clasping a temporary delay rather than an escape. Maintain the position patiently and use small incremental hip bridges to gradually break the grip. You can also peel the clasping hand using your free hand while maintaining hip pressure, or walk your hips higher to increase the lever angle against the clasped grip.

common_errors.error: Releasing the overhook before the leg is fully positioned over the opponent's head
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recovers posture immediately and either extracts the arm or stacks forward to pass guard
common_errors.correction: Maintain the deep overhook until your calf is fully seated across the back of the opponent's neck - only then begin transitioning your overhook grip to wrist control

common_errors.error: Incomplete belly down rotation leaving the attacker on their side rather than fully prone
common_errors.consequence: The opponent retains stacking angles and can drive into the half-rotated attacker to extract the arm or sweep to top position
common_errors.correction: Commit fully to the rotation by driving your hips through to face completely toward the mat - your chest and face should end pointing straight down, not to the side

common_errors.error: Loose knee squeeze during the rotation phase allowing the arm to shift position
common_errors.consequence: The opponent's elbow slides off the hip fulcrum, eliminating the hyperextension angle and allowing them to bend the elbow and escape
common_errors.correction: Maintain maximum adductor squeeze throughout the entire rotation, actively pinching your knees together as your primary focus during the turn

common_errors.error: Jerking or spiking the arm extension for the finish rather than applying gradual progressive pressure
common_errors.consequence: Extremely high risk of serious elbow injury including ligament rupture and joint capsule damage, especially since the belly down position amplifies force significantly
common_errors.correction: Apply extension through slow controlled hip elevation, progressively increasing pressure over 2-3 seconds and pausing at each increment to allow time for the tap

common_errors.error: Attempting the belly down rotation without first establishing perpendicular hip angle
common_errors.consequence: The rotation is mechanically inefficient, requiring excessive effort and creating windows where the opponent can extract the arm during the awkward transition
common_errors.correction: Hip escape to create a 90-degree angle to the opponent's body before initiating the belly down turn - this alignment makes the rotation smooth and maintains arm isolation throughout

common_errors.error: Losing wrist control during the belly down rotation by gripping too loosely
common_errors.consequence: Opponent bends their elbow immediately during the rotation, neutralizing the armbar entirely and potentially escaping to top position
common_errors.correction: Establish a firm two-on-one wrist grip before rotating and pull the wrist tight against your chest throughout the turn - the wrist should never separate from your body during rotation

training_progressions.focus: Belly down rotation and finishing pressure
training_progressions.description: Practice the belly down rotation from a standard armbar position without the New York entry. Partner provides no resistance. Focus on smooth rotation, maintaining knee squeeze, and applying gradual hip extension pressure. Complete 30 repetitions each side per session until the rotation feels natural and automatic.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 2: New York to armbar chain
training_progressions.focus: Connecting New York control to armbar isolation
training_progressions.description: From established New York, practice the complete sequence of shooting the leg over, clamping the arm, securing wrist control, and completing the belly down rotation. Partner provides light resistance. Focus on timing the overhook release to coincide with leg positioning and maintaining control through every transition point.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining the finish against defensive reactions
training_progressions.description: Partner actively defends using arm extraction attempts, stacking, hitchhiker escape, and hand clasping. Practice responding to each counter while maintaining position. Drill specific counter-to-counter sequences until you can adjust instinctively to each defensive reaction without losing the submission position.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 4: Positional sparring from New York
training_progressions.description: Start from New York bottom with partner at full resistance. Attempt the belly down armbar as one option within your New York attack tree. Alternate between committing to the armbar and switching to other attacks based on the opponent's reactions. Develop the ability to read which defensive reaction opens the armbar versus other submissions.

Integrate the belly down armbar from New York into full sparring rounds. Practice finding the position organically from rolling, not just from set starts. Train the technique during late-round situations when grip strength is diminished to develop reliable finishing mechanics under fatigue conditions.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structure does the belly down armbar from New York primarily attack and why is the belly down position particularly dangerous for this target?
flashcards.answer: The primary target is the elbow joint, specifically hyperextending it to stress the ulnar collateral ligament and joint capsule. The belly down position is particularly dangerous because the prone orientation creates a mechanical advantage ratio exceeding 5:1 against the elbow joint. Unlike a standard supine armbar where the attacker must lift their hips against gravity, the belly down position allows gravity to assist the extension force, meaning even small hip elevations generate significant hyperextension pressure. This amplified leverage means damage can occur much faster than practitioners expect.

trap: Sit up and crank the shoulder

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts pulling their trapped elbow back toward their hip during the transition from overhook to leg clamp - what adjustment prevents the escape?
flashcards.answer: Do not chase the retracting arm. Instead, maintain the deep overhook pressure and use your leg that was crossing their back to immediately hook over their shoulder, creating a secondary barrier to extraction. If their arm is partially extracted, transition to a triangle setup since their arm withdrawal creates the inside position needed for the triangle lock. If the overhook is still deep enough, re-consolidate New York control and wait for a better opening rather than forcing a compromised armbar attempt.

flashcards.question: What is the correct grip configuration on the opponent's wrist during the belly down finish and why does it matter?
flashcards.answer: Use a two-on-one grip with both hands wrapping the wrist, thumbs pointing toward the opponent's fingers and palms overlapping around the wrist. Pull the wrist tight against your chest so it maintains contact with your sternum throughout the rotation. This grip configuration matters because it prevents the opponent from bending their elbow to relieve hyperextension pressure. A single-hand grip or a loose two-hand grip allows enough wrist rotation for the opponent to turn their arm and find extraction angles during the belly down rotation.

plausible: One hand grip, other on hip
trap: Crank their fingers to hold on

flashcards.question: Your opponent clasps their hands together to defend the arm extension after you have completed the belly down rotation - what is your finishing strategy?
flashcards.answer: The belly down position makes hand clasping a delay rather than an escape. Maintain patient position and use small incremental hip bridges to gradually stress the grip until it breaks. Alternatively, use one hand to peel the clasping fingers while maintaining hip pressure with the other hand controlling the wrist. You can also walk your hips slightly higher toward the opponent's shoulder to increase the lever angle, which multiplies force against the clasped grip without requiring additional strength. Never rush or jerk against a clasped grip as this risks injury.
flashcards.answer_line: Small hip bridges break the grip

trap: Let go of the wrist to pry hands

flashcards.question: What is the critical fulcrum point for the belly down armbar finish and how do you verify it is correctly positioned?
flashcards.answer: The critical fulcrum is the line of your hip bones pressing against the back of the opponent's elbow. Verify correct positioning by feeling the bony point of their elbow directly against your hip crease before initiating finishing pressure. If the elbow is too high (toward your waist), the lever is inefficient and the opponent can resist. If too low (toward your thighs), you risk the arm slipping free during extension. The correct position is confirmed when a very small hip bridge produces immediate and clear pressure on the opponent's elbow joint.
flashcards.answer_line: Hip bone on back of elbow

trap: Lift hips to hunt the elbow

flashcards.question: During the belly down rotation, your opponent attempts a hitchhiker escape by rotating their thumb toward the mat - how do you counter this?
flashcards.answer: Follow their rotation by adjusting your hip angle to stay perpendicular to their upper arm rather than their body. Squeeze your knees tighter to prevent the arm from rotating within your thigh clamp. The belly down position actually makes the hitchhiker significantly less effective than against a standard supine armbar because your body weight pins their shoulder, preventing the full body rotation the hitchhiker escape requires. If they persist, walk your hips slightly in the direction of their rotation to re-center the elbow against your hip fulcrum.

plausible: Follow their body, not the arm
trap: Open knees to chase the rotation

flashcards.question: Why must you establish a perpendicular hip angle before initiating the belly down rotation and what happens if you skip this step?
flashcards.answer: The perpendicular hip angle is essential because it aligns your rotation axis with the arm isolation plane. Without this angle, rotating belly down requires you to simultaneously turn and reposition, creating a complex movement where the arm can shift off the hip fulcrum. Skipping this step typically results in either losing wrist control during an awkward rotation, the opponent's elbow sliding to an ineffective position between your thighs, or the rotation stalling at the halfway point where the opponent can stack and extract their arm.

flashcards.question: What are the key safety protocols when applying the belly down armbar finish in training?
flashcards.answer: Apply extension through slow, controlled hip elevation over 2-3 seconds minimum, never jerking or spiking the arm. The belly down position amplifies force far beyond what most practitioners expect, so what feels like light pressure to the attacker may produce serious hyperextension for the defender. Release immediately upon any tap signal. Practice the rotation and the finishing pressure as separate components until both are controlled. Never apply this technique on partners with known elbow injuries. Beginners should work at 50% pressure maximum until control is consistent.

plausible: Drill rotation and finish as one
Judge pressure by your own feel
trap: Spike hips fast for a quick tap

flashcards.question: How should you release the belly down armbar after receiving a tap signal?
flashcards.answer: Release extension pressure first by lowering your hips back to the mat and dropping the wrist downward, removing all hyperextension force from the elbow immediately. Then release your knee squeeze to free the arm from the thigh clamp. Finally, disengage completely by rolling off and creating space. Do not release in reverse order because opening the knees while maintaining wrist tension can cause the arm to jerk into a different hyperextension angle. Monitor your partner's arm mobility after release and check for signs of injury before continuing training.
flashcards.answer_line: Drop hips and wrist, then knees

flashcards.question: In competition, your opponent is defending intelligently by keeping their elbow bent and posture low - what strategy forces the opening for the belly down armbar from New York?
flashcards.answer: Use attack cycling to force a defensive error. Threaten the triangle by shooting your leg over their shoulder, then when they defend the triangle by posturing their head back, their trapped arm straightens momentarily as they redirect defensive effort. This straightening creates the window to clamp the arm and initiate the belly down rotation. Alternatively, use a hip bump to off-balance them forward, forcing them to post with their free hand, which isolates the overhook arm for the armbar entry. The key is making the armbar the second threat in a chain, not the first.

trap: Crank the bent elbow to force it

defender.name: from New York Defender
defender.description: Defend the belly down armbar from New York rubber guard. Recognize setup cues, prevent arm isolation, extract before rotation, and recover guard safely.
defender.overview: Defending the belly down armbar from New York requires early recognition of the attacker's shift from guard retention to arm isolation. The transition from New York overhook to armbar configuration creates a narrow but critical window where extraction is still possible before the attacker completes the belly down rotation. Once the rotation is complete, defensive options become severely limited due to the extreme mechanical disadvantage of the prone finishing position. Defensive priority must be on preventing the rotation itself through posture recovery and arm extraction rather than attempting to escape after the belly down position is fully established, because the 5:1 leverage ratio of the completed position makes muscular escape nearly impossible regardless of strength differential.
key_principles: Early recognition is survival - once the belly down rotation is complete, escape probability drops below 15%
Protect the elbow angle by keeping the arm bent at all times during escape attempts rather than straightening to push away
Posture recovery before arm extraction - without posture, pulling the arm free is mechanically impossible against a deep overhook
Stack the attacker when possible during the rotation phase to disrupt their belly down transition and create extraction angles
Tap early and without hesitation if the belly down position is fully locked - the mechanical advantage makes damage extremely rapid
Use the free hand to grip-fight the attacker's shin-controlling hand, creating openings for posture recovery
recognition_cues: Attacker releases their shin grip and begins swinging their outside leg upward toward your head or neck from New York
Attacker's hips elevate and angle perpendicular to your body while maintaining the deep overhook, indicating arm isolation setup
Attacker shifts from pulling your head down to controlling your wrist with both hands, signaling transition from guard control to submission
Attacker's leg crosses over your shoulder or neck creating the closed leg configuration around your trapped arm
You feel rotational pulling on your trapped arm as the attacker begins turning face-down toward the mat

defensive_options.when_to_use: Early phase when the attacker is still in New York control before they shoot the leg over your head - this is your primary prevention window
defensive_options.if_successful: Return to New York top position with posture partially recovered, forcing attacker to re-establish control before attempting again
defensive_options.risk: If extraction fails, the arm pulling motion may create the angle the attacker needs to shoot their leg over more easily

defensive_options.action: Stack and drive forward during rotation
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has begun the belly down rotation but has not completed the full turn - their transitional position is vulnerable to forward pressure
defensive_options.if_successful: Flatten the attacker and disrupt the rotation, allowing you to extract the arm and settle into closed guard top position
defensive_options.risk: Driving forward against a fully locked belly down position is futile and wastes energy that could be spent tapping or addressing the submission

defensive_options.action: Hitchhiker escape by rotating toward trapped arm
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the belly down rotation is partially complete but the attacker has not yet established firm wrist control with both hands
defensive_options.if_successful: Rotate your body in the direction of the trapped arm's thumb, spinning free of the leg clamp and recovering to closed guard or scrambling to top position
defensive_options.risk: The belly down position limits hitchhiker effectiveness compared to standard armbar defense - if the attacker follows your rotation, the escape fails and you remain trapped

defensive_options.action: Hand clasp and elbow bend defense
defensive_options.when_to_use: Last resort when the belly down rotation is complete and you cannot escape the position - buy time to create a micro-opening
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the immediate tap and creates time to find an extraction angle, though the position remains deeply unfavorable
defensive_options.risk: This is a temporary delay, not an escape - the attacker's mechanical advantage will eventually break the clasp, and prolonged resistance risks sudden elbow damage when the grip fails

escape_paths: Extract the trapped arm by pulling the elbow back toward the hip while the attacker transitions from overhook to leg clamp, recovering to New York top or closed guard
Stack and drive forward during the rotation phase to flatten the attacker and disrupt the belly down turn, then withdraw the arm and settle into closed guard top
Hitchhiker escape by rotating the thumb toward the mat and spinning the body toward the trapped arm before the attacker secures full wrist control

favorable_outcomes.how: Stack the attacker during the rotation phase to prevent the belly down completion, extract the trapped arm as forward pressure disrupts their leg clamp, and settle into closed guard top where the rubber guard threat has been neutralized

Extract the trapped arm early before the leg shoots over by pulling the elbow back and recovering posture, returning to New York top position where the attacker must restart the entire setup sequence from guard control

common_errors.error: Attempting to muscle out of the belly down position after the rotation is complete using pure strength
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy rapidly without creating meaningful escape opportunity, and the sudden muscular effort against the locked position can cause self-inflicted elbow injury as the arm straightens explosively into the hyperextension
common_errors.correction: Recognize that a completed belly down armbar has extreme mechanical advantage that strength cannot overcome - tap immediately if the position is fully locked rather than fighting a losing battle that risks injury

common_errors.error: Straightening the trapped arm to push the attacker away during the transition phase
common_errors.consequence: A straight arm is exactly what the attacker needs for the hyperextension finish, effectively completing their submission for them
common_errors.correction: Keep the elbow bent at all times by pulling the hand toward your own chest or grabbing your opposite bicep - a bent arm cannot be hyperextended and creates the structural resistance needed to find extraction angles

common_errors.error: Ignoring the early recognition cues and not reacting until the leg is already over the head
common_errors.consequence: The defense window closes rapidly once the leg is positioned across your neck, leaving only low-percentage escape options against the imminent belly down rotation
common_errors.correction: React immediately when you feel the attacker release their shin grip or begin elevating their hips - these are the earliest warning signs and the point where prevention is still high percentage

common_errors.error: Failing to tap when the belly down position is fully locked with tight knee squeeze and two-on-one wrist control
common_errors.consequence: The extreme mechanical advantage of the completed belly down position means elbow damage can occur within 1-2 seconds of extension beginning, risking serious ligament injury or fracture
common_errors.correction: Tap immediately and without hesitation when you feel the belly down rotation complete and your arm fully trapped - there is no shame in tapping to a mechanically superior position, and the position can be drilled to improve defense in future encounters

flashcards.question: How do you recognize the belly down armbar from New York is being set up before the leg crosses over your head?
flashcards.answer: The earliest cue is the attacker releasing their shin grip while maintaining the deep overhook, indicating they are transitioning from guard retention to submission setup. You will also feel their hips begin to elevate and angle perpendicular to your body as they create space for the leg swing. Their focus shifts from pulling your head down to controlling your wrist area. React immediately to these cues by fighting for posture recovery and pulling your elbow back toward your hip before the leg completes its path over your head.

trap: Wait until the leg crosses over

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap when caught in a fully locked belly down armbar?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately using multiple signals simultaneously: verbal tap saying 'tap' clearly, physical hand tap on the attacker's body or the mat with your free hand, and foot tap on the mat with either leg. Use all available signals because the prone position may muffle verbal taps and limit the attacker's ability to feel hand taps. Do not wait to see if you can escape first - the belly down position creates extreme leverage that can cause serious elbow damage within 1-2 seconds of extension pressure beginning. Tapping early preserves your training longevity.
flashcards.answer_line: Use voice, hand, and foot at once

plausible: Single hand tap on the mat
trap: Ride it out and hunt an escape

flashcards.question: What is the highest-percentage defensive window during the belly down armbar transition from New York?
flashcards.answer: The highest-percentage window is between the attacker releasing their shin grip and their leg fully crossing over your head. During this 1-2 second window, the attacker's control structure is temporarily weakened because they have abandoned the shin control that maintained New York but have not yet established the leg clamp for the armbar. Use this window to explosively recover posture by driving your head upward and pulling your trapped elbow back toward your hip. If you miss this window, the next opportunity is during the belly down rotation before wrist control is secured, but this is significantly lower percentage.
flashcards.answer_line: Between shin release and leg cross

flashcards.question: What defensive options remain after the attacker has completed the belly down rotation?
flashcards.answer: Options are very limited once the rotation is complete. Hand clasping by grabbing your own wrist or bicep can delay the finish temporarily but will eventually fail against the mechanical advantage. The hitchhiker escape by rotating your thumb toward the mat and spinning has reduced effectiveness against belly down compared to standard armbar but may work if the attacker's wrist control is imperfect. Realistically, if the belly down position is fully locked with tight knees and two-on-one wrist control, the correct response is to tap immediately rather than risk injury fighting an unwinnable position.

plausible: Pull the trapped arm straight out

flashcards.question: How do you prevent the initial arm isolation from New York that leads to the belly down armbar?
flashcards.answer: Prevent arm isolation by addressing it at the source: fight the deep overhook by keeping your elbow tight to your body and working to extract it through grip fighting on the attacker's overhook hand. Maintain as much posture as possible within New York by widening your base and using your free hand to frame against the attacker's hip. When you feel the attacker begin releasing their shin grip (the earliest transition cue), immediately pull your trapped elbow back toward your hip and drive your head upward for posture. The goal is making the overhook shallow enough that the attacker cannot maintain arm control through the leg transition.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying setup cues from New York
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes New York and cycles through various attacks including the belly down armbar setup. Defender calls out which attack is being initiated as soon as they recognize the cues. No physical defense yet, purely pattern recognition. Build the ability to distinguish belly down armbar setup from triangle, omoplata, and other New York attacks within the first second of initiation.

Partner initiates the belly down armbar from New York at moderate speed. Defender focuses exclusively on the early prevention window by recovering posture and extracting the arm before the leg crosses over the head. Partner resets if defender succeeds. Track success rate to measure improvement and identify which extraction timing works best against different attacker body types.

Partner has already shot the leg over and is initiating the belly down rotation. Defender practices stacking defense and hitchhiker escape during the rotation phase. Work both options to develop instinctive selection based on the attacker's body position and wrist control quality. Accept that success rate will be lower than early prevention and focus on reading which defense has the higher percentage in each specific scenario.

Full positional sparring from New York with partner attacking at competition speed. Defender implements complete defensive strategy from early recognition through last-resort defenses. Emphasize appropriate tap timing when the position is fully locked rather than fighting unwinnable positions. Develop the judgment to distinguish between escapable and locked positions under live pressure.

clips.title: Countering rubber guard control and its attacks
